# Data science

A discipline module, not a stack module — owns the workflow method, not
Python/R syntax. Combine with whichever stack conventions skill matches
the current repo for language and framework conventions — they ship
into a repo as `.claude/skills/<id>/SKILL.md` and
`.cursor/rules/<id>.mdc`, and only for the stacks that repo uses.

## Reproducibility

- Pin the environment (lockfile, not a loose requirements list) —
  "works on my machine" is not reproducible
- Set and log every random seed that affects the result: split,
  initialization, shuffling, sampling
- A result that can't be regenerated from the logged config + seed is
  not a result yet, it's an anecdote

## Data validation before training

- Check schema, null rates, and class balance before anything trains
  on the data, not after a confusing result shows up
- Confirm the train/validation/test split has no leakage — no shared
  entities, no target information encoded in a feature, no future data
  in a time-series split
- A silently-changed input distribution is the most common cause of a
  model that "used to work" — check for it before debugging the model

## Experiment tracking

- Every run logs its config, metrics, and artifact (model/plot/output)
  together — a metric without the config that produced it is
  unreproducible and not worth recording
- Compare against a real baseline (the current production model, or a
  trivial heuristic) — an isolated accuracy number means nothing on
  its own

## Evaluation

- Pick the metric the business decision actually depends on, not
  whichever one is easiest to compute — accuracy on an imbalanced
  class problem is close to meaningless
- Check performance on the specific segments that matter (not just
  the aggregate) — an aggregate win can hide a regression on the
  segment someone actually cares about
- State the uncertainty (confidence interval, error bars), not a bare
  point estimate, when the sample size is small enough that it matters

## Notebook-to-production

- Notebooks are for exploration; anything that runs in production goes
  through the same review/test discipline as any other code — no
  notebook cells shipped as-is
- No hardcoded paths, credentials, or environment-specific values
  anywhere near what eventually ships
